title: Dispersion Table — rich
forward_vector: I am the manifest of Dispersion Table's rich face, its first round, still a proposal: four walks that climb to what the page claims about the loop and its filter slot (a wavetable is a lossless loop, exactly, and a fractional length already fills the slot; partials land where the round trip comes to whole turns; the two axes of the table; one allpass knob from pure through piano to bell), the Dissolutions proof the first walk climbs to, and the Waveguide Synthesizer's own stiffness tour beside the warp knob. I grow when Loudon has heard them; I never hold the entry's words.

pieces.file: Dispersion Table — rich — the table and the loop.html
pieces.title: the table and the loop · a walk in four steps
pieces.caption: **Is a wavetable a lossless loop, and does a fractional length really put a filter in it?** The table alone, a reader sweeping a stored cycle; the loop alone, the cycle sliding past a still tap; their difference, which is zero at every sample (and stops being zero when the loop is one sample longer, so the test can fail); and last the loop made half a sample longer. There it has to read between samples on every trip, and the reading is a filter either way: a straight line, which at a half sample is Karplus-Strong's average, takes level (harmonic 10 at 110 Hz loses about 2.5 to 2.9 dB a second, the table none); an allpass keeps level and takes timing (at 1760 Hz the top harmonics sit 22 to 23 cents flat of the table's; this is an allpass of half a sample after P whole ones, coefficient +⅓. The Wavetable Oscillator's face splits the same length as 99 + 1.5, coefficient −0.2, and that split bends them sharp instead, so the two faces agree). Measured from the rendered loop at 44.1 and 48 kHz, within 0.006 cents of the round-trip condition. Not heard by the agent that made it.
pieces.near: A delay line fed back on itself with unity gain

pieces.title: the table that travels · the Dissolutions proof
pieces.caption: **The proof the walk above climbs to, gathered as it was.** Its three doors (the table, the loop, their difference) and its loop filter, eight first-order allpasses, with the partials followed to where the round-trip condition sends them. Loudon played it on 2026-10-25 and asked for the steps before it: the table alone, the loop alone, the two combined through their difference, then the filter. The walk above is those steps. Its notes keep only in this viewer.

verdicts.file: Dispersion Table — rich — the table and the loop.html
verdicts.why: Tests the identity (difference 0 exactly, live at P + 1) and that a fractional length fills the slot either way; walks up on Loudon's own outline. Note: 'flat' is this split's sign (delay ½, coefficient +⅓); the Oscillator's 99 + 1.5 split bends sharp (+0.955 ¢ at h10, reproduced), so the caption should name the split.
The proof the walk climbs to, placed as its last step and gathered as it was; tracked, storage contract in the manifest, conform clean.

pieces.file: Dispersion Table — rich — where the partials land.html
pieces.title: where the partials land · a walk in four steps
pieces.caption: **Do the partials land where the round trip comes to whole turns, and what takes them off the grid?** The condition drawn as a count of turns against frequency: a straight line for the bare loop; a steeper straight line for Karplus-Strong's average, where the Waveguide Synthesizer walk ends (the pitch drops to fs ⁄ (N + ½), the series stays harmonic); a bent line for eight first-order allpasses; and last each loop rendered and measured. The partials sit on the crossings within 0.003 Hz. A lag that grows in a straight line only retunes; one that bends moves partial 12 tens of cents off. Here θ(f) is drawn as a lag, positive for a delay. Not heard by the agent that made it.

verdicts.file: Dispersion Table — rich — where the partials land.html
verdicts.why: Renders three loops and measures partials against the crossings (within 0.01 Hz), and tests what the section implies: a straight lag retunes by fs/(N+½), only a bent one leaves the grid (+39 ¢ at partial 12, the default). Walks bare, straight, bent, measured.

sections.heading: From one curve to a table

pieces.file: Dispersion Table — rich — two knobs, one loop.html
pieces.title: two knobs, one loop · a walk in four steps
pieces.caption: **Do the table's two axes stay apart?** A magnitude knob alone (a three-tap lowpass whose phase is a straight line), a phase knob alone (the page's eight allpasses), the two as a square you click to pluck, and last the test, at 110 and 440 Hz. In the filter they are apart. In the sound they are not quite: a one-pole brightness knob, the usual one, moves the pitch (measured with the bare delay held, so a retune could take that back) and bends the partials a few cents against each other at 440 Hz, which no retune removes; and the phase knob changes how fast partials die, a lot at 440 Hz, because decay is loss per trip times trips per second. Predicted from the engine and checked against the rendered string. Not heard by the agent that made it.

verdicts.file: Dispersion Table — rich — two knobs, one loop.html
verdicts.why: A real test of the two axes, and its findings recompute (6.90/6.26 ¢ pitch, 2.7–3.2 ¢ bend, partial 4 38→90 and 32→73 dB/s). Note: the pitch move is with the bare delay held, which a retune removes; say in the caption that the bend is what survives.

pieces.file: Dispersion Table — rich — the warp knob.html
pieces.title: the warp knob · a walk in four steps
pieces.caption: **Does one pole radius walk the loop from pure, through piano, to bell?** One second-order allpass (level one everywhere, a click smeared in time); eight in log steps, 300 Hz to 12 kHz, whose delay curve is what a table would store; the eight in a Karplus-Strong string at 110 Hz; and last the knob swept 0 to 0.97 and sorted. The page's recipe reads pure to about 0.22, piano to 0.90 (B from 2e-6 to 2.4e-4), then irregular, the low partials falling flat as the high ones go sharp. That is where the page puts its bell, but it is a new shape, not a wider spread: about 141 cents at its widest at 0.97, against 106 at the top of the piano band. Eight identical first-order sections, the stiff string's recipe, only ever stretch. Whether the irregular end sounds like a bell is left to the ear: no agent has heard it.
pieces.near: A cascade of second-order allpass sections

pieces.title: the stiffness tour · the same knob, built
pieces.caption: **The stiff string's recipe in a built instrument.** G3 plucked at stiffness 0, 0.4, 0.7 and 1.0, two seconds each, then C3 up to C5 at 0.7: harmonic, to piano-like, to a struck bar. Its engine uses first-order allpasses, designed per note so one stiffness means one stretch at every pitch (study v1.10's own notes say one fixed coefficient had stretched A5 about 800 times more than E2). It stretches; it never turns irregular, as the walk above predicts for that recipe.
pieces.near: A cascade of second-order allpass sections

verdicts.file: Dispersion Table — rich — the warp knob.html
verdicts.why: Tests the one-knob claim with stated band rules and a first-order contrast; walks one, eight, string, sweep. Note: 'the page's bell end' over-maps; the irregular end is a new shape, not a wider spread (about 141 ¢ at 0.97 against 106 ¢ at the piano band's top), so say that.

A witness rather than a test: the stretch-only recipe heard in a built instrument; caption matches stiffness-tour.json and the study's 800× note, and the ladder is monotone at every take the tour plays. Tracked, the palace's own render.

offers.what: The page calls θ(f) 'the loop filter's phase response' and adds it to 2πfτ as accumulated phase. In the usual convention a filter's phase response is negative for a delay, so the θ in the equation is the phase lag: the phase response with its sign turned. The piece draws it that way. Suggested: '(the loop filter's phase lag θ(f), its phase response with the sign turned so a delay counts positive)'.

The page's claim held, exactly: a whole-sample loop and the table give the same samples, difference 0 over 3 s at 110, 440 and 1760 Hz, three shapes, 44.1 and 48 kHz; one sample longer, they part. The piece adds which filter the fractional slot holds, depending on how the loop reads between samples. A straight line takes level and keeps timing: at a half sample it is Karplus-Strong's average, and harmonic 10 at 110 Hz loses 2.5 to 2.9 dB a second while the table loses none. A first-order allpass keeps level and takes timing. Split as P whole samples plus an allpass of half a sample (coefficient +⅓), it bends the harmonics flat: the top harmonic it keeps sits 0.015 to 0.019 cents flat at 110 Hz (harmonic 24), 1.06 to 1.40 at 440, and 22 to 23 cents flat at 1760 (harmonic 11 or 12), the range across 44.1 and 48 kHz. The sign belongs to the split: the Wavetable Oscillator's face splits 100.5 as 99 + 1.5 (coefficient −0.2), whose group delay falls with frequency, and bends them sharp (+0.955 cents at harmonic 10; +28.6 to +30.5 at 1760 Hz). Both faces are right; the page's wording should stay neutral ('bends the tuning'). Suggested addition after 'is already a filter in the loop': 'Read between samples by a straight line, it takes level (at a half sample, it is Karplus-Strong's average); read by an allpass, it keeps level and bends the tuning, the first dispersion curve in the slot.'

offers.section: From one curve to a table
offers.what: The page never says the two axes are independent; it says what each governs. In § The identity it rests on the magnitude response 'governs brightness and decay rate', and here the position axis selects 'brightness, decay rate'. In the sound, decay is not the magnitude's alone. A partial's decay per second is its loss per trip times its trips per second, and the trips are the phase axis's: at 440 Hz, darkness 0.6, sweeping the warp 0 to 0.9 takes partial 4 from 38.2 to 90.4 dB a second (44.1 kHz; 32.4 to 73.1 at 48), 2.37 times faster: the partial moves up 301 cents to where each trip takes 1.40 times more, and its trip shortens from 100 to 59 samples, 1.70 times the trips a second. At 110 Hz the change is about 0.1 dB a second. The other way, the magnitude axis leaves the partials alone only if its filter's phase is a straight line: a three-tap lowpass moves none (0.000 cents). A one-pole set to darken partial 8 as much, being minimum-phase, cannot: with the bare delay held it lowers the pitch 1.46 to 1.59 cents at 110 Hz and 6.26 to 6.90 at 440, which a retune takes back, and bends the partials 2.7 to 3.2 cents against each other at 440 Hz, which no retune removes. Cross-Domain Resonance's 'magnitude on one axis, phase on the other' is about the filter and true as written. Suggested, on the two 'governs decay' lines: 'decay rate, which the phase axis shares, since a partial's trips a second follow its delay'.

offers.section: From one curve to a table
offers.what: One stored curve does not select one inharmonic structure across the keyboard. On the page's recipe at warp 0.8 (8 sections, 300 Hz to 12 kHz, centres fixed in Hz), the fitted B over 12 partials is about 1.5e-5 to 1.7e-5 at 55 Hz, 1.2e-4 to 1.3e-4 at 110, 8.7e-4 to 9.9e-4 at 220 and 7.3e-3 to 8.7e-3 at 440 (48 and 44.1 kHz): eight times per octave, 493 to 521 times over three octaves: B grows as the cube of the pitch (fitted exponent 2.93 to 3.01). Below the sections' features the stored lag is about τ₀ω + cω³; over a trip of N samples, partial k moves by about −c(2πk)²/N³, so B ∝ 1/N³ ∝ f₀³, 512 over three octaves. Two powers come from a higher note's partials sitting higher on the same curve, the third from the same lag shared over a shorter trip. At 0.5: 1.5e-6 to 1.8e-6 at 55 Hz up to 6.6e-4 to 8.0e-4 at 440. The Waveguide Synthesizer met the same thing (study-v1.10 index.html, the v1.5 comment: one coefficient for eight sections 'stretched A5 about 800 times more than E2', 3.42 octaves, exponent 2.83, the same law bending as the high partials leave the cubic range) and now designs its dispersion per note. Found by the engine and by reading the study, not by a piece step. Suggested: a clause that a table stored against frequency stretches high notes far more than low ones, so to mean one inharmonicity at every pitch its curves are keyed to the note.

The order held; the strong spread did not. On the page's recipe at 110 Hz (the bands move with pitch, by the offer before), 24 partials, 44.1 and 48 kHz: pure (every partial within 1 cent) to 0.21 to 0.24; piano (a stretch that follows fn = n f0 √(1 + B n²) within a tenth of its spread) from there to 0.90, B from 2e-6 to 2.4e-4; irregular (low partials flat while high ones go sharp) from 0.91 to 0.97. The top is a new shape, not a wider spread: about 141 cents at its widest at 0.97, against 106 at the top of the piano band, where the page says 'strong inharmonic spread'. And it needs the second-order sections. Every allpass's phase rises with frequency; what decides the shape is its group delay. A first-order section's group delay is monotone in frequency, and so is a sum of identical ones, so eight identical first-order sections (the stiff string's recipe, and the Waveguide Synthesizer's) only stretch: piano to about 0.70, then past the piano's law toward a stiff bar, never irregular. A second-order section's group delay peaks at its centre, and log-spaced peaks are what send low partials flat while high ones go sharp. Whether the irregular end sounds like a bell or a gong is untested by ear. Suggested: say the knob ends in a new shape at the top tenth of the radius, and that it is the second-order sections' centres that make it.
